story.title: Supreme Court Blocks Trump-Backed Congressional Map in Missouri
story.summary: The Supreme Court has rejected a Missouri congressional map backed by Trump and Republicans for the third time, preventing its use in the upcoming midterm elections. This ruling halts a federal appeals court decision that aimed to revive the Republican-friendly map, which was intended to give the party an electoral advantage. The justices issued their decision without any noted dissents.

Instead, the state must revert to a 2022 congressional map. This marks the second time the Court has intervened in Missouri's redistricting efforts, which have been contentious over the past year.

event_overview.title: About Redistricting
event_overview.subject: Redistricting
event_overview.summary: This event concerns an emergency-election dispute over which Missouri congressional district map governs the 2026 U.S. House election. Missouri enacted a replacement map in 2025, but the state supreme court held that a valid referendum petition prevented it from taking effect unless voters approve it; the U.S. Supreme Court subsequently stayed federal orders that would have required use of the 2025 map.

facts.label: Jurisdiction and offices affected
facts.value: The litigation concerns Missouri’s boundaries for elections to the U.S. House of Representatives, rather than Missouri legislative districts.

facts.label: Maps at issue
facts.value: Missouri enacted a congressional map in 2022 and another in 2025; the state supreme court concluded that the 2022 map remained in force for the November 2026 general election unless the 2025 measure was approved by voters through the referendum process.

facts.label: Referendum rule
facts.value: Missouri’s constitution permits a referendum on most laws when petitions meet the required signature threshold in at least two-thirds of the state’s congressional districts and are filed within 90 days after adjournment of the legislative session that passed the law.

facts.label: Key state-court ruling
facts.value: On September 3, 2026, the Supreme Court of Missouri ruled in von Glahn v. Hoskins that the referendum petition challenging the 2025 congressional-redistricting act was legal, sufficient, and timely.

facts.label: Federal emergency posture
facts.value: On September 25, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court stayed specified district-court and Eighth Circuit orders and directed that lower federal courts not prohibit use of the 2022 map or require use of the 2025 map while the stays remain in effect.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the Supreme Court’s September 2026 emergency interventions over Missouri’s map for the 2026 election, not the full history of Missouri redistricting, the referendum campaign, or every related state and federal court proceeding.

explore_lenses.label: What map will Missouri use, and what changed?
explore_lenses.title: The 2022 districts govern the November election
explore_lenses.summary: The immediate change is administrative, not a final nationwide ruling on mid-decade redistricting: Missouri must conduct its 2026 general election under its 2022 congressional map rather than the Legislature's 2025 map.

claims.text: The U.S. Supreme Court said the Missouri Supreme Court's interpretation of state law means the 2025 map cannot take effect unless voters approve it by referendum; therefore, the 2022 map must be used for the 2026 congressional election.

The 2025 map had been used in the August primary, but the Supreme Court noted that ballots using the 2022 map had already been printed and mailed and that absentee, military, and overseas voting had begun.

The redesigned 5th District centered on Kansas City was the principal political change: it extended into rural Republican areas, and an AP estimate found that about 59% of its voters would have been new under the 2025 map.

explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: The Court's order decides which map is used for the November 3, 2026 election; it does not permanently resolve every constitutional argument about changing maps between a primary and general election.
explore_lenses.note: Researched context; forecasts and viewpoints are labeled and attributed.

explore_lenses.label: Why did the Court reject the primary-map argument?
explore_lenses.title: Timing and election administration controlled
explore_lenses.summary: Supporters of the 2025 map argued that using different maps for the August primary and November general election violated federal constitutional protections. The Supreme Court said that proposition was not clearly established and concluded that changing course after voting had begun would create unacceptable disruption.

claims.text: The Eighth Circuit held that the Constitution did not permit Missouri to use a different congressional map in the November general election than in the August primary, and ordered implementation of the 2025 map.
The Supreme Court said its precedents had not previously held that Article I, Section 2 requires a state to use its primary-election map in the general election, so the merits were not clear-cut.

The Supreme Court applied its election-timing doctrine, reasoning that reverting to the 2025 map during an election already underway would cause electoral disorder; it cited local election officials' assessment that reverting was practically impossible at that point.

Secretary of State Denny Hoskins argued that retaining the 2025 map would keep primary nominees and general-election voters in the same districts, calling that outcome necessary for orderly election administration.

explore_lenses.label: What happens after the November election?
explore_lenses.title: Voters will decide whether to approve the 2025 map
explore_lenses.summary: Missouri voters will see the redistricting law itself on the November 3 ballot while voting for Congress under the 2022 districts. The referendum's result, rather than this emergency order alone, determines whether House Bill 1 can take effect afterward under the Missouri Supreme Court's state-law ruling.

claims.text: Missouri's official ballot-measures page lists Proposition A for the November 3, 2026 general election and asks whether voters approve House Bill 1, which repeals the existing congressional plan and replaces it with new boundaries.
The official ballot language states that a 'yes' vote approves the redrawn districts, while a 'no' vote leaves the 2022 congressional boundaries in place.

The Missouri Supreme Court held that the referendum petition was legal, sufficient, and timely; it ordered the measure placed on the November ballot and concluded that HB 1 does not take effect unless approved by voters.

story_report.summary: The U.S. Supreme Court blocked a Trump-backed, Republican-supported Missouri congressional map for a third time, preventing it from being used in the 2026 midterm election. The Court said the Missouri Supreme Court’s reading of state law requires voter approval before the 2025 map can take effect, leaving the 2022 boundaries in place for the Nov. 3 election. The 2025 plan had already been used in the August primary, but voting under the earlier map was already underway.

sections.heading: Election Timing Dispute
sections.body: The Eighth Circuit had ordered Missouri to implement the 2025 map, concluding that the Constitution did not permit the state to use different congressional maps for the August primary and November general election. The Supreme Court said its precedents had not previously established such a requirement and found that switching back to the 2025 map during an election already in progress would create electoral disorder. It cited local officials’ assessment that a reversal was practically impossible after ballots had been printed and mailed and absentee, military and overseas voting had begun.

sections.heading: Kansas City District Changes
sections.body: The principal political change in the 2025 plan was a redesign of the 5th District centered on Kansas City. The district would have extended into rural Republican areas, and an Associated Press estimate found that about 59% of its voters would have been new under the proposed map. Secretary of State Denny Hoskins argued that retaining the 2025 boundaries would have kept primary nominees and general-election voters in the same districts, which he described as necessary for orderly election administration.

sections.heading: Proposition A Faces Voters
sections.body: Missouri voters will decide Proposition A on Nov. 3. The ballot measure asks whether to approve House Bill 1, which repeals the existing congressional plan and replaces it with new boundaries; a yes vote approves the redrawn districts, while a no vote retains the 2022 boundaries. The Missouri Supreme Court ruled that the referendum petition was legal, sufficient and timely, and held that HB 1 cannot take effect without voter approval.

unresolved.text: The Supreme Court’s order determines the map for the 2026 election but does not finally resolve the underlying constitutional claims. The reviewed sources also do not establish precisely when new boundaries would take effect after a Proposition A victory or whether further litigation would follow.

related_stories.title: Trump Dismisses Iran's Proposal to Reopen Strait of Hormuz
related_stories.summary: President Donald Trump has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within a week and resume nuclear negotiations. The proposal, submitted through Qatar, included a condition for lifting the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports. Trump stated, 'They made a proposal but I reject it,' indicating expectations of renewed military actions following the midterm elections.

related_stories.title: Lawmakers Criticize Trump's $810 Million Funding Cut as Unlawful
related_stories.summary: The White House announced plans to cut $810 million in funding that had been approved by Congress, prompting bipartisan criticism from lawmakers who labeled the move as unlawful. This action marks a rare use of authority by the Trump administration to rescind nearly $1 billion in previously allocated spending.

related_stories.title: White House Denies CNN Access to Cover Trump's Tennessee Trip
related_stories.summary: The White House has barred CNN from covering President Trump's upcoming trip to Tennessee, preventing the network from joining him on Air Force One. This decision follows a recent court order that restored CNN's access to the White House after a previous ban. The move is seen as part of ongoing tensions between the Trump administration and the news network.

related_stories.title: TikTok Settles Alabama Lawsuit Over Youth Safety for $100 Million
related_stories.summary: TikTok has agreed to pay at least $100 million to settle a lawsuit filed by Alabama regarding the platform's impact on youth mental health. The settlement, which avoids an impending trial, includes commitments to implement new safety measures for teenage users, such as usage limits and enhanced parental controls.
